name: Fish-scale pearlescent lip color

card.summary: A lip shimmer made from guanine crystals once harvested from fish scales, giving lips a glossy, pearly sheen.
card.note: Modern pearl lip products mostly use mica or other pigments; guanine can irritate eyes.

quick.overview:
Fish-scale pearlescent lip color uses guanine, the crystalline substance in fish scales, to give lips a pearly, light-catching shimmer. The same material has been used since the 1600s to create imitation pearl effects.

The thin layered crystals partly reflect and partly pass light, producing a soft luster that makes lips look fuller and glossier. Modern shimmer products more often use mica or other pearl pigments, with guanine as a traditional or specialty ingredient.
quick.how: Users apply it as a shimmer or gloss over or in place of lip colour, usually as a pearly topper that catches light. It is typically found as part of cosmetic formulas rather than as a stand-alone raw material.
quick.risks: Guanine crystals can irritate the eyes, and alternatives such as mica exist for people who avoid animal-derived ingredients. Standard cosmetic patch-testing and allergy cautions apply.

lead: Fish-scale pearlescent lip color refers to lip shimmer based on guanine, the crystalline compound that gives fish scales their silvery iridescence. It is applied to give lips a pearly glow that appears to shift with light.

Guanine-based "pearl essence" has a long cosmetic history. It was reportedly extracted from the scales of the bleak fish in Paris in 1656 and identified as guanine in 1861, and it has been used in shimmer products, nail polish, eye shadow and imitation pearls.[1]

Guanine crystals are thin, transparent platelets with a high refractive index, so layers of them reflect and transmit light to create pearly luster.[1] Today mica, ground faux pearl and metal particles are common alternatives.[1]

angle.text: The crystals give lips a pearly, reflective finish. People wear it as a highlight over lip colour to make lips catch the light.

paras: The use of guanine for pearl-like effects goes back to 1656, when a Parisian reportedly extracted pearl essence from bleak scales; guanine was identified as its active component in 1861.[1]
Guanine forms thin, layered, transparent crystals with a high refractive index. Light is partly reflected and partly transmitted between layers, producing the pearly luster.[1]
Guanine can irritate the eyes, and animal-derived sources lead some buyers to choose mica or synthetic pearl pigments.[1]
